saa-med-037.text: A health company needs to prove in audits who accessed specific objects of a pocket S3 with records — including object reading operations (GetObject), which do not appear on the standard path of the CloudTrail. Which configuration captures these accesses?
options: The standard trail of CloudTrail already records all readings of objects
Enable data events of S3 no CloudTrail for the pocket of medical records
Enable Bucket Version to Record Readers
Use Amazon Macie to record each reading
saa-med-037.explanation: The default track records management events; operations at object level (GetObject, PutObject) are data events and need to be explicitly enabled — generating the required data access track in audits.
saa-med-037.hint: Administrative actions and touchdowns DADOS are different categories in CloudTrail — the second one needs to be linked to the part.
optionRationales: The default track records management events; operations at object level (GetObject, PutObject) are data events and need to be explicitly enabled — generating the required data access track in audits.
Justly not: event at object level are separate category (data events), disabled by default by volume and cost.
Versioning tracks content versions, not who read the objects.
The Macie classifies sensitive data stored — does not work as a request access audit trail.

saa-med-038.text: A team identified that it needs to encrypt card data before it even sends them to AWS, keeping the keys under your control in the client, so that the provider never sees the content in clear. As this encryption model is called, in contrast to the encryption on the server side?
options: SSE-S3, because the keys stay with the client
Encryption in transit TLS, which keeps the data encrypted also in storage
Customer-side encryption: the data is encrypted in the application before shipment and deciphered only by it
Hashing data with SHA-256 before shipment
saa-med-038.explanation: In client-side encryption, the application encrypts data with keys it controls (own or via KMS) before transmission — the service stores only encrypted material, without ever accessing the content in clear.
saa-med-038.hint: If the provider can never see the content, encryption needs to happen ANTES from leaving the house.
optionRationales: In client-side encryption, the application encrypts data with keys it controls (own or via KMS) before transmission — the service stores only encrypted material, without ever accessing the content in clear.
TLS only protects the transmission channel — the data is clearly sent to the service, which then applies (or does not) own encryption.
No. SSE-S3 the encryption occurs on the server with keys managed by itself S3 — the opposite of total control in the client.
Hash is irreversible and serves for integrity verification — card data need to be recoverable, which requires encryption, not hashing.

saa-med-039.text: A database RDS production needs to continue to respond even if the Availability Zone where it rotates becomes unavailable, with automatic failover and no changes in the connection string of the application. Between Multi-AZ and Read Replicas, which feature meets this requirement and why?
options: Multi-AZ, because it keeps a synchronous replica in standby on another AZ and performs automatic failure while preserving the same endpoint
Read Replicas, because they take over the mains place automatically in seconds
Automatic snapshots, because they restore the bank instantly in the same AZ
ElastiCache in front of the bank, which assumes the writings if the RDS fall
saa-med-039.explanation: Multi-AZ is the high availability resource of RDS: synchronous replication for the instance in wait and automatic failure with the same endpoint DNS — the application reconnects without changes.
saa-med-039.hint: Think of what resource the RDS offers automatic failover preserving the same endpoint, instead of just scaling readings.
optionRationales: Multi-AZ is the high availability resource of RDS: synchronous replication for the instance in wait and automatic failure with the same endpoint DNS — the application reconnects without changes.
Reading replicas use asynchronous replication and DO NOT automatically promote themselves — promotion is manual and generates a new endpoint; their purpose is to scale readings.
Snapshot Restore creates a new instance in lengthy process — it is not automatic failover nor maintains the endpoint.
Cache does not replace the bank in writing — without the RDS, transactions would simply fail.

saa-med-040.text: A cluster Amazon Aurora has a record instance and two replicas Aurora in different AZs. If the record instance fails, what happens and what endpoint the application should use to benefit from this?
options: The replicas continue to serve only readings and the writings are suspended forever
The Aurora automatically promotes one of the replicas to the label in seconds, and the application should use the endpoint cluster (writer), which starts pointing to the new label
The cluster is unavailable until a snapshot is manually restored
The application needs to manually change the IP address of the bank in the code
saa-med-040.explanation: The failover of Aurora promotes a replica (typically in less than 30 seconds, because the storage is shared) and updates the endpoint cluster automatically — applications that use this endpoint recover without reconfiguration.
saa-med-040.hint: No. Aurora, the storage is shared between the instances — the promotion is fast and the 'writing' endpoint accompanies who became the holder.
optionRationales: The failover of Aurora promotes a replica (typically in less than 30 seconds, because the storage is shared) and updates the endpoint cluster automatically — applications that use this endpoint recover without reconfiguration.
With replicas available, the failover is automatic — manual restoration would only be required without any replica and no backtrack.
Automatic promotion converts a replica to a record — the writings return after the failover.
The use of the endpoint cluster eliminates this maintenance: the DNS of the endpoint follows the current record label automatically.

saa-med-041.text: An application rotates in one Auto Scaling Group behind a ALB. The instances pass in the status check of EC2, but sometimes the application process stops and stops responding HTTP, without Auto Scaling what adjustment makes the group replace instances whose APPLICATION has failed.?
options: Manually restart the instances stopped every day
Increase the time of health check grace period
Change the ALB by one NLB
Configure the Auto Scaling Group to use the type health check ELB, considering not healthy the instance failed in the health check of the balancer
saa-med-041.explanation: With health check type ELB, o ASG begins to consider the vision of the balancer (which tests the answer HTTP of the application) and replaces instances whose process has stopped — something that the status check of the EC2 (infrastructure) does not detect.
saa-med-041.hint: The EC2 see hardware; the balancer sees or HTTP — which view the group should adopt to replace locked applications?
optionRationales: With health check type ELB, o ASG begins to consider the vision of the balancer (which tests the answer HTTP of the application) and replaces instances whose process has stopped — something that the status check of the EC2 (infrastructure) does not detect.
The grace period only gives more time for lack of initialization — does not change the source of integrity verification.
Changing the type of balancer does not change the criterion used by ASG to decide replacements.
Recurrent manual intervention is just what health checks automation eliminates.

saa-med-042.text: A critical application rotates in a Auto Scaling Group distributed in 3 Availability Zones with 6 The architect wants to ensure that if an entire AZ fails, the remaining capacity still meets 100% of peak load. Which sizing practice meets this requirement?
options: Provide extra capacity (N+1 by AZ), so that the remaining AZs add up the capacity needed for peak even if they lose a zone
Use only instances Spot for contingency capacity
Reduce the minimum capacity to save and scale only after failure
Focus all instances on the most reliable AZ
saa-med-042.explanation: Static resilience: sizing so that the loss of an AZ still leaves sufficient capacity (e.g. each pair of AZs responds to peak) avoids relying on emergency launches during failure — when capacity in the Region may be contested.
saa-med-042.hint: Plan for 'one less': the fleet must withstand the peak even with a zone out of the game.
optionRationales: Static resilience: sizing so that the loss of an AZ still leaves sufficient capacity (e.g. each pair of AZs responds to peak) avoids relying on emergency launches during failure — when capacity in the Region may be contested.
Focusing on a single zone creates exactly the single point of failure that multi-AZ distribution eliminates.
Trust in Scaling DURANTE disaster is risky: recovery is dependent on provisioning under stress, with possible lack of capacity.
Spot can be recovered by AWS at any time — inadequate as the sole guarantee of capacity in a failure scenario of AZ.

saa-med-043.text: A service HTTP internal is served by 8 In this case, the team wants the DNS respond with up 8 healthy IP addresses, automatically removing those that fail in health check, distributing customers among others. What a routing policy of Route 53 offers this behavior?
options: Geolocation rotation
Multivalue rotation answer with health checks associated with each record
Simple routing with multiple IPs in the same record
CNAME pointing to each instance sequentially
saa-med-043.explanation: The multivalue answer returns multiple healthy records (up to 8) by consultation, excluding failings in health checks — a simple form of distribution with verification of integrity via DNS.
saa-med-043.hint: It is the policy that returns 'various answers' by consultation — only those that passed the health examination.
optionRationales: The multivalue answer returns multiple healthy records (up to 8) by consultation, excluding failings in health checks — a simple form of distribution with verification of integrity via DNS.
Simple routing does not support health checks — dead server IPs would continue to be delivered to customers.
Geolocation chooses answers by the customer's geographical origin — does not remove unhealthy endpoints from a server pool.
One CNAME points to a single name per record — does not distribute among multiple targets with integrity check.

saa-med-044.text: One-row consumers SQS processing videos that lead to 10 With the standard visibility timeout of 30 seconds, messages reappear in the queue before processing is finished and end up being duplicated by other consumers.?
options: Change the Standard row to a topic SNS
Delete messages immediately upon receipt before processing
Decrease visibility timeout to release messages faster
Increase the row's visibility timeout to a value greater than the maximum processing time (ex: 12 minutes)
saa-med-044.explanation: The visibility timeout should cover the processing time: while in effect, the message becomes invisible to other consumers, avoiding duplication; the consumer excludes it when concluding.
saa-med-044.hint: The 'invisibility' of the message must last at least as long as the work takes.
optionRationales: The visibility timeout should cover the processing time: while in effect, the message becomes invisible to other consumers, avoiding duplication; the consumer excludes it when concluding.
Reducing timeout would exacerbate the problem by multiplying duplicate reappearances and processing.
SNS is push without retention for consumption at its own pace — does not solve long processing visibility control.
Excluding before processing definitely loses the message if the consumer fails in the middle — sacrifices reliability.

saa-med-045.text: An insurance company has defined for its system of policies RTO of 30 minutes and RPO of 5 in the event of a regional disaster, with a budget that does not involve running duplicate production in total capacity. What DR strategy balances these objectives and the cost?
options: Warm standby: a functional version in reduced scale running in the secondary region with continuously replicated data, scaled to full size during failure
Backup & Restore with daily backups
No DR strategy, relying on the Multi-AZ of the main region
Active-active multi-site in total capacity
saa-med-045.explanation: Warm standby keeps the environment complete, but reduced, always active with continuous replication — failover in minutes (television RTO of 30 min) and minimum data loss (takes care of RPO of 5 (min) by fraction of the cost of the asset-asset.
saa-med-045.hint: Between the 'pilot name' and the 'complete mirror' there is the middle term: everything is connected, only in small size.
optionRationales: Warm standby keeps the environment complete, but reduced, always active with continuous replication — failover in minutes (television RTO of 30 min) and minimum data loss (takes care of RPO of 5 (min) by fraction of the cost of the asset-asset.
Daily backups involve RPO up to 24 hours and RTO hours to rebuild everything — far beyond the set goals.
The active-active would meet the metrics with a break, but the double production cost was explicitly discarded by the budget.
Multi-AZ does not protect against disaster REGIONAL — the requirement requires presence in second Region.

saa-med-046.text: A global financial system uses Amazon Aurora and requires that, in a regional disaster, the bank be available in another region with RPO of about 1 second and RTO of a few minutes. Aurora was designed for this requirement?
options: Aurora Global Database, with replication between regions in typical latency below 1 second and rapid promotion of the secondary region
Manual snapshots copied to another region every hour
Continuous export to CSV in a pocket S3 local
Aurora Multi-AZ with three replicas in the same region
saa-med-046.explanation: The Aurora Global Database replicates to Secondary Regions in the typical storage layer with a delay of less than a second, and the secondary can be promoted in minutes — RPO ~1s e RTO low for regional DR.
saa-med-046.hint: The name of the resource delivers at scale: the 'global' bank of the Aurora with second level replica between regions.
optionRationales: The Aurora Global Database replicates to Secondary Regions in the typical storage layer with a delay of less than a second, and the secondary can be promoted in minutes — RPO ~1s e RTO low for regional DR.
Hourly copies imply RPO up to 1 time and prolonged restoration — orders of magnitude above required.
Replicas in the same region do not survive a disaster REGIONAL — the requirement is geographical.
Exports to file are not bank failover mechanism — recovery would require slow and loss-prone reimportation.

saa-med-047.text: A table of the DynamoDB has been accidentally excluded from mass items by a faulty script. The team needs to restore the table to the exact state of 10 minutes before the incident. What resource allows this recovery?
options: DAX, which saves items in the cache
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR), which allows to restore the table for any second of the last 35 days
Global Tables, which keep copies in other regions
Increase reading capacity to recover deleted items
saa-med-047.explanation: With PITR enabled, or DynamoDB keeps continuous backups and allows to restore for any instant in the hold window — recovering the state immediately prior to the faulty script.
saa-med-047.hint: To 'return in time' to the second exact before the disaster, what a continuous backup resource the DynamoDB offers?
optionRationales: With PITR enabled, or DynamoDB keeps continuous backups and allows to restore for any instant in the hold window — recovering the state immediately prior to the faulty script.
Global Tables replicate TODAS changes — including undue exclusions, which would spread to replicas in seconds.
The DAX is volatile reading cache — is not backup mechanism or data restoration deleted.
Readability does not recover deleted data — deleted items no longer exist to be read.

saa-med-048.text: A global application needs users to continue reading and recording data from DynamoDB even if an entire region of AWS stay out of the air, with redirection of traffic to another Region without intervention in the bank. What resource provides this active-active architecture?
options: DynamoDB Global Tables, with multi-active replicas synchronized automatically between regions
Export the table to S3 with replication between regions
PITR with restoration in the other region during the incident
An instance RDS of replica for the DynamoDB
saa-med-048.explanation: Global Tables keep replicas with reading and writing in multiple Regions, automatically replicated: in the failure of one Region, just traffic is directed to another replica, which already accepts written.
saa-med-048.hint: For writing in any region with automatic synchronization, the DynamoDB has its 'global' tables'.
optionRationales: Global Tables keep replicas with reading and writing in multiple Regions, automatically replicated: in the failure of one Region, just traffic is directed to another replica, which already accepts written.
Restoring backups during disaster generates hours of RTO and loses recent writings — is not active architecture.
Exports are static copies for analysis — do not provide an active bank for real-time failure.
RDS and DynamoDB are distinct and incompatible services — there is no replica RDS of a table DynamoDB.
